title: Architectural Principles of the Internet
subtitle: The foundational design philosophy behind the Internet's architecture

eli5.summary: Nobody drew a master plan for the Internet, so this note writes down the rules of thumb that turned out to work: keep it simple, let the computers at the two ends do the clever work, and expect everything to keep changing.

questions: what are the architectural principles of the internet
what is the end to end principle
what does be strict when sending and tolerant when receiving mean
why should internet protocols be kept simple

tldr.problem: The Internet grew by evolution rather than from a Grand Plan, so its design rules existed only as unwritten tradition.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB records a snapshot of guidelines: connectivity is the goal, the Internet Protocol is the tool, and the intelligence lives at the ends of the network (the end-to-end argument), so state is kept at the endpoints.
tldr.outcome: A numbered checklist (heterogeneity, scalability, simplicity, running code, names and addresses, security) for judging new protocol designs. It is explicitly not dogma or a formal reference model.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Connectivity is the goal, IP is the tool, intelligence is end to end

facts.label: Rule 3.14
facts.value: Nothing gets standardised until there are multiple instances of running code

today: The IAB later revisited the list in RFC 3439, which updates this document, and wrote about the pressure that middleboxes put on end-to-end design in RFC 3724 and RFC 4924. The ideas here still shape protocol review: end-to-end security, "keep it simple", "nothing is standardised without running code" and the warning that today's sacred principle may be deprecated tomorrow.

hero.subtitle: The foundational design philosophy behind the Internet's architecture

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes the fundamental architectural principles that guided the design of the Internet. These principles explain why the Internet works the way it does and provide guidance for future protocol design.

Understanding these principles is essential for anyone designing Internet protocols or distributed systems. They represent decades of collective wisdom about building scalable, resilient networked systems.
sections.eli5: Nobody designed the Internet from a master plan, like a town that grew one street at a time. This note is a list of the rules of thumb that helped most, and it says right at the start that the rules themselves will keep changing.

sections.title: Core Principles
sections.content:
Packet Switching
The RFC (section 2.3) concludes that datagrams are better than classical virtual circuits: the network's job is to transmit datagrams as efficiently and flexibly as possible, and everything else should be done at the fringes.
Fate Sharing
An end-to-end design should not rely on state about the communication being held inside the network. Such state should be kept only in the endpoints, so that it can only be destroyed when the endpoint itself breaks.
Heterogeneity Support
Item 3.1 says heterogeneity is inevitable and must be supported by design, with transmission speeds differing by at least 7 orders of magnitude and hosts from memory-starved microprocessors up to massively parallel supercomputers.
No Central Control
Section 2.4 says nobody owns the Internet, there is no centralized control, and nobody can turn it off. Its evolution depends on rough consensus and running code.
sections.eli5: Send things in small separate packets, keep the notes about a conversation with the two people talking and not with the post office in the middle, let any kind of wire or radio carry it, and remember that nobody is the boss of the whole thing.

sections.title: The End-to-End Argument
sections.content:
Perhaps the most important principle: functions should be implemented at the endpoints of a communication, not in the intermediary network nodes. The network should be kept simple and general-purpose.

The RFC (section 2.3) quotes Saltzer, Reed and Clark: "The function in question can completely and correctly be implemented only with the knowledge and help of the application standing at the endpoints of the communication system. Therefore, providing that questioned function as a feature of the communication system itself is not possible." An incomplete version provided by the network may still be useful as a performance enhancement.

Endpoint Function
Network Function
Error correction
Best-effort delivery
Flow control
Routing
Encryption
Forwarding
Application logic
Addressing
sections.eli5: If you want to be sure a letter arrived, the post office cannot do that for you, because only you and your friend can check. So the roads just carry things, and the people at the two ends do the checking.

sections.title: Simplicity and Generality
sections.content:
The Internet architecture values simplicity and generality. Protocols should be designed to be as simple as possible while still meeting requirements.

Postel's Law
Item 3.9: "Be strict when sending and tolerant when receiving." Implementations must follow specifications precisely when sending, and tolerate faulty input from the network, silently discarding it when in doubt. This robustness principle is often credited to Jon Postel.
Minimal Design
Item 3.5: "Keep it simple. When in doubt during design, choose the simplest solution." Item 3.8 adds that options and parameters should be avoided whenever possible.
Modularity
Item 3.6: "Modularity is good. If you can keep things separate, do so." Section 2.2 adds that the Internet-level protocol must be independent of the hardware medium and hardware addressing.
sections.eli5: When there are two ways to build something, pick the easier one. When you send, follow the rules carefully. When you receive something a bit odd, do not make a fuss.

sections.title: Layering
sections.content:
RFC 1958 does not define a layer model of its own; the layers below are the common textbook view. What it does say (section 2.2) is that, ideally, there is one and only one protocol at the Internet level, and that this protocol must be independent of the hardware medium and hardware addressing, so the Internet can exploit any new transmission technology.

Other levels may have multiple protocols for different requirements; the single Internet-level protocol is what lets different transmission media interconnect.
sections.eli5: Like a stack of boxes: each box does one job and trusts the box under it. The one in the middle, IP, is the part that lets every kind of wire talk to every other kind.

sections.title: Universal Connectivity
sections.content:
The Internet was designed to provide universal connectivity - any host should be able to communicate with any other host. Section 2.1 states the goal as connectivity, and the RFC calls connectivity its own reward. Later documents such as RFC 2775 discuss how NATs and firewalls erode it.

The RFC itself does not mention NAT. It does say (item 6.2) that confidentiality and authentication are the responsibility of end users, and that endpoints should not depend on the confidentiality or integrity of the carriers.
sections.eli5: The big idea is that any computer can reach any other computer. Some modern gadgets get in the way of that, and people keep working on ways to fix it.
